newsitem.title: FRANCE: Europe loosening drink ad rules as U.S. gets tough.
newsitem.headline: Europe loosening drink ad rules as U.S. gets tough.

text.p: As U.S. President Bill Clinton gets tough on American drinks firms for advertising on television, Europe's strict rules on alcohol commercials are loosening up.

Clinton on Tuesday sought a study on curbing television liquor ads after the drinks industry ended a nearly 50-year-old ban, saying television ads "would provide a message of encouragement to drink that young people simply don't need".

In Britain a voluntary ban on advertising spirits on television ended last year with no political or public outcry. At Christmas the small screen was filled with adverts vaunting seasonal cheer through whisky and cognac.

Belgium now allows advertising of drinks of up to 20 percent alcohol in strength rather than 10 percent after the European Commission rapped it over the knuckles last year, saying the rule favoured domestically-brewed beer over imported wine.
But perhaps the biggest onslaught on tight rules governing drinks adverts comes in France, where a law dating from 1993 prohibits all alcohol and tobacco advertising.
When the law was passed, broadcasters decided not to show sporting events from other countries if adverts for French drinks could be seen in foreign stadiums.

France is under pressure from American brewer Anheuser Busch, a sponsor of the World Cup football tournament which takes place in France next year, either to exempt it from the law or to interpret the law less harshly in time for the event.

"We believe it was never the intention of French lawmakers to place such restrictions on advertising that appears in other countries, yet that is the unfortunate effect of the law in this situation," Anheuser president and chief operating officer Stephen Burrows said in a recent statement.

Anheuser has involved sports, health and culture ministries in its bid to be able to put posters advertising its Budweiser beer on panels at World Cup events, and its chairman has written to French President Jacques Chirac over the matter.
However, it got no joy from a bid to involve the European Commission in its battle. The Commission last month dropped Anheuser's complaint against France.

"There is a risk of a completely crazy situation, where the World Cup will take place but could not be broadcast in France," said Jacques Bille, chairman of the French ad agency group Association des Agences Conseils en Communication (AACC).
France faces two other complaints, one from Bordeaux wine makers and another from European beer brewers, which could land it in the European Court of Justice.

In this case, the European Commission has asked France to justify its restrictions on broadcasting certain sporting events, saying they contravened European rules on free circulation of goods and services. The French government is working on a reply.
"We think the law is out of proportion to its objectives," AACC's Bille said, adding that Europe's single market could not function properly under existing French law on alcohol adverts.

Drinks industry, sports and advertising lobbyists are gnawing away at anti-alcohol advertising laws on the grounds that they contravene European Union rules which stipulate that goods and services should circulate freely in all member states.
Unlike tobacco, wine gets a good health ticket in France, a major wine exporter.
The industry, hit by a 15-year decline in wine drinking among the French which is just starting to show signs of a reverse, takes every opportunity to show how wine can be good for you.

A recent study suggested that wine can help prevent Alzheimers' disease or senile dementia. The French wine industry also boasts that red wine helps stave off heart attacks which could be caused by eating too much rich food, red meat and foie gras.
